body: Originally called the imitation game, the Turing test is meant to determine whether a computer or AI can think like a human being. The test consists of a human interviewing both a person and machine. The machine passes the Turing test if the interviewer cannot correctly identify which is the machine and which is the person.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Turing test." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 28, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Ben Laposky produces the first graphics generated by electronic machines, a critical step on the way to the digitization of generative art with proto-computer art.

Using an oscilloscope in 1950, Ben F. Laposky originated the concept of graphics generated by electronic machines, creating his now legendary oscillons. These “electrical compositions” are regarded as among the first electronic graphics.
Image is copyrighted by Ben Laposky and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

img.credit: Spalter Digital. 2023. Electronic Abstraction 4. spalterdigital.com

body: The Molnárs were forced to leave Vera’s bourgeois family estate to make room for a relative and his young girlfriend, who had an unexpected pregnancy and needed to marry right away. Given some money for rent, Vera and François were confronted with the harsh realities of Parisian real estate. They found a one-room apartment in Belleville “with a tiny kitchen and the toilet on the landing. Horrible. But we still drew and it still worked. We survived,” she later recollected. When asked at the time where she lived, Vera replied, “You wouldn’t believe me; it’s horrendous. Belleville.”

cite.label: Peter Bauman, “Molnár’s Paris,” Le Random, 26 February 2024, section 3. Belleville Apartment. Includes Vera Molnár’s recollections from Interview with Vincent Baby (Manuella éditions, 2022), p. 37, quoted in the article.

img.cap: Belleville, Paris, 1952. Period view of the neighbourhood where Vera and François Molnár lived; not identified as their exact home.
img.credit: Photograph: Keystone-France / Gamma-Keystone. Reproduced in Peter Bauman, “Molnár’s Paris,” Le Random, 2024. Image source.
img.alt: Cobbled Belleville street in 1952 with a handcart, worn buildings, and a pedestrian beside a fence.
creator: Keystone-France / Gamma-Keystone

body: This major Venezuelan kinetic artist and abstract geometric painter began his collage work with found materials inspired by Mondrian. These would lead to one of his significant contributions, Coloritmo (Colorhythms).

img.cap: Alejandro Otero, Ortogonal (Collage) 2, 1951. Cut-and-pasted colored paper on cardboard.
img.credit: Alejandro Otero. Courtesy of the Otero Pardo Foundation. Digital Image © 2020 The Museum of Modern Art, New York / Licensed by SCALA / Art Resource, NY. Reproduced by The Art Newspaper, 2022. Image source.
img.alt: Overlapping horizontal and vertical paper strips in black, gray, yellow, red, purple and green, with the source’s color chart and MoMA credit below.

body: A seminal figure in the development of Kinetic Art, Soto’s arrival in Paris put him in contact with Victor Vasarely, Yaacov Agam, Jean Tinguely and others connected with the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles. The pioneer of kinetic and optical art, characterized by geometric shapes and movement, used simple shapes and colors to create visually engaging artworks, paving the way for computer-generated art.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Jesús Rafael Soto." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified January 14, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Beginning in September 1951, Edmund C. Berkeley published Computers and Automation, the first magazine dedicated to the computing revolution. Next decade, Computers and Automation would play a vital role in the development of computer art with its “Computer Art Contest” beginning in 1963.

The Hungarian-American mathematician von Neumann’s conception of cellular automata (CA), suggested by Stanislaw Ulam, demonstrated the potential for simple rules to give rise to complex and unpredictable behavior. CA has been foundational to the development of generative art as CA profoundly influenced fields such as artificial life, complexity science, and computer graphics.

Mathematician Ivan Moscovich experimented with different mechanisms to create complex curves and shapes based on mathematical formulas. His work demonstrated the potential of algorithmic processes to generate intricate and visually appealing designs. Moscovich’s work was an early example of the intersection between mathematics, computer programming, and art.

cite.label: Taylor, Grant D. When the Machine Made Art: The Troubled History of Computer Art, 70. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2014.

img.cap: Ivan Moscovich, Harmonograms of Moscovich, 1968. Analog-computer original, 24 × 24 inches. A later example of the mathematical forms he began exploring in the 1950s.
img.credit: Ivan Moscovich. Artist-submitted reproduction for the 2010 Bridges Conference, Mathematical Art Galleries / The Bridges Organization. Reproduction photographer not identified. Image source.
img.alt: Dense curved blue and black lines form a rounded, twisting harmonogram with pink, cyan and yellow arcs on white.
creator: Ivan Moscovich

body: SNARC (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator), the first artificial neural network, was composed of simple electronic circuits that could learn from their environment and adjust their behavior accordingly. Using 3,000 vacuum tubes to simulate a network of 40 neurons, it paved the way for the development of modern machine learning and artificial intelligence.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Marvin Minsky." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 27, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Based on its prototype, the legendary Manchester Mark I, the Ferranti Mark I was the world’s first commercially available general-purpose digital computer.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Ferranti Mark 1." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 17, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Meaning “Experimental Workshop” in English, Jikken Kobo was a radically experimental Japanese art collective, with a highly Deleuzian approach to art and the technology of the time. They created groundbreaking works that integrated technology, music, performance and visual art, using electronic devices and new media to create innovative and immersive experiences for their audiences. At the time in the early ’50s, this was one of the most radical art movements in the world.

img.cap: A 1954 group portrait of the Jikken Kōbō members in a Tokyo courtyard — fourteen figures in winter coats, three years after the collective formed.
img.credit: Members of Jikken Kōbō (Experimental Workshop), 1954. Via Monoskop.

body: The singular pioneer of generative music, John Cage began to utilize chance in his compositions around this time with “Imaginary Landscape No 4″ and “Music of Changes.” In “Imaginary Landscapes,” twelve radios were played at once with their broadcasts determined by chance and out of Cage’s control.

img.cap: John Cage, Imaginary Landscape No. 4 (or March No. 2), 1951. Cover of the current Edition Peters full score, EP 6718; printing date unspecified.
img.credit: John Cage; Henmar Press / Edition Peters. Publisher’s product image. Image source.
img.alt: White score cover headed Cage and Imaginary Landscape No. 4 for 12 radios, 24 players and conductor, with the Edition Peters imprint.
creator: John Cage

body: Composed during his time in France, this part of a series of chance-arranged spectrum collages marked the shift of Kelly’s work towards chance methodologies as well as work on a grid. Inspired by Dadaism and Surrealism, this preeminent example of chance in art has strongly influenced later generations of generative artists as well as bearing conceptual and form resemblance to the color chart work of Gerhard Richter.

img.credit: Rob Corder. “Spectrum Colors Arranged by Chance, 1951. Oil on wood (1923-2015) SFMOMA.” Flickr. flickr.com

body: A pioneering work in the development of proto-computer abstract animation, Around Is Around, made with Evelyn Lambart and Chester Beachell, is a ten-minute long animated film that was groundbreaking for its time. It used an oscilloscope to produce certain abstract images, one the first published animations to do so.
The British Film Institute expounds:

“This experiment blazes so many trails that we need to list them before considering which is merely a picturesque by-path, and which may be expected to lead some where. Among the more important novelties exemplified are:

(i) Three-dimensional abstract form.  (ii) Abstract form plus stereophonic music.  (iii) Abstract form produced from hand-drawn track photographed frame-by-frame.  (iv) Abstract form produced by normal-speed cinematography.  (v) Three-dimensional form produced by synthesis from a series of two-dimensional images.”

img.cap: A frame from Around Is Around showing one of the Lissajous figures McLaren and Evelyn Lambart photographed directly off an oscilloscope screen.
img.credit: Norman McLaren, Around Is Around, 1951. © National Film Board of Canada.

body: Begun in the mid-1940s under Jay Forrester at MIT to drive a programmable flight simulator for the Office of Naval Research, Whirlwind was demonstrated processing live radar data in September 1950. The Whirlwind is a significant step in the evolution of computing technology as it was the first computer that could display real-time graphics and text with its oscilloscope screen. The computer would last until 1959 when it was finally shut down due to its large costs.

img.cap: A rack unit from MIT's Whirlwind computer, photographed against black — the machine's chassis, not its oscilloscope display.
img.credit: Whirlwind computer unit, MIT. From 'Computation and the Transformation of Practice', MIT Libraries Digital Humanities Lab, via the Internet Archive.

body: Kicking off the Neo-Dada movement and critical to the development of performance art, Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1 paved the way for the movement’s collaborative, multimedia and chance-based nature. The piece included several simultaneous, improvized performance elements including a poetry reading, music, dance, photography, film and plastic work (four panels of Robert Rauschenberg’s White Paintings hung from the ceiling). Other than assigning the mediums, Cage “let each individual artist determine the specifics of their role within the performance, emphasizing the function of chance in determining the course of the event.”

img.cap: The main Studies Building of the former Black Mountain College at Lake Eden, North Carolina — the campus where Cage staged Theater Piece No. 1 in the dining hall in summer 1952 — photographed in 2007 on the grounds of Camp Rockmont.
img.credit: Photograph of the former Black Mountain College Studies Building, Lake Eden, North Carolina. Wikimedia Commons, released into the public domain by the photographer.

body: A landmark in the history of computer-generated text, Strachey’s love letter algorithm (or M.U.C.) created generative poems by combining words selected from a database via the random generator of the Ferranti Mark I.
It anticipates the combinatorial procedures the computer artists of the ’60s, among them Noll, Nake and Nees, would arrive at independently.
Besides its massive importance in the development of information theory and the computer art of the ’60s, Love-Letters remains pivotal to how we think about digital generative art today.
Sasha Stiles writes of this event’s importance:

“In collaboration with Alan Turing, programmer Christopher Strachey creates an automated love-letter generator for the Manchester Mark I computer [the Ferranti Mark 1] – the world’s first experiment in text-generating software.”
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript).

cite.label: Gitelman, Lisa. "Review of Archaeology of Algorithmic Artefacts, by David Link." Computational Culture, no. 6 (2017).

img.credit: "Computer Love" by NightCity85 is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 2.0. To view a copy of this license, visit creativecommons.org.

body: The Independent Group (IG), a collective of British artists, critics, and designers who came together in the early 1950s, explored the intersection of pop culture, mass media imagery, and art in technology. They sought to bridge the gap between high art and popular culture and were interested in the impact of new technologies on art and society. IG members Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi would go on to infulence computer art again in the early ’70s influence Slade to adopt technology in art’s teaching. Thus, they were a principal group in the surge of participatory and technological art of the ’50s and ’60s whose influence extends far beyond. The group’s members, including Hamilton, John McHale, Paolozzi and Alison and Peter Smithson, even paved the way for the Pop Art movement and influenced contemporary art and design. Hamilton, McHale and Paolozzi were in particular interested in art’s mechanization. IG’s collage work juxtaposed art and technology in a way that was revelatory and radical at the time. The group’s vision to anticipate both mass media and digital art make them critical touchstones in the history of the mechanization of art and, thus, on-chain generative art.

Pioneering work of abstract electronic animation Using an oscilloscope, Bute was the creator of some of the earliest electronically generated images. In 1952, she created the landmark experimental film Abstronic, (a portmanteau of the words “abstract” and “electronic”). Her abstract animations anticipated the upcoming aesthetic language of computer art by incorporating Lissajous curves and geometric abstraction. Bute was captivated by the proposition of drawing with light. She revealed that with only knobs and switches “I can ‘draw’ with a beam of light with as much freedom as with a brush.” In fact, she “would rather use light to draw with instead of making thousands of drawings.” Bute was one of the first people in history to recognize that when a human and electronic instrument collaborate, “the creative possibilities are limitless.”

img.cap: Mary Ellen Bute observing an image on the oscilloscope screen whose knobs and switches she used to “draw with a beam of light” for Abstronic (1952).
img.credit: Mary Ellen Bute / Ted Nemeth. Collection of Center for Visual Music, Los Angeles.

body: While not formally named until the early 1960s by Barbara Rose, we consider the birth of Neo-Dada to have occurred in 1952 with John Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1. This seminal, multi-media, collaborative work of performance art involved unscripted poetry, music and Robert Rauschenberg’s White Painting (1951), four panels of which hung above the performers. These elements would all become hallmarks of the Neo-Dada movement in the coming years. Paving the way for Pop Art, Minimalism and Conceptualism, the term Neo-Dadaism was applied to the works of artists such as Jasper Johns, Merce Cunningham, John Cage, Robert Rauschenberg and Allan Kaprow. Marcel Duchamp’s arrival in New York and increasing influence can partially explain the movement’s genesis. Neo-Dada artists are known for their usage of mass media, found objects and performance. Most importantly for generative art, Neo-Dada was known for its embrace of chance, from Kaprow (performance) to Cunningham (dance) and Cage (music). In this sense, Neo-Dada was profoundly impactful on contemporary generative art. It was also a predecessor to the digital mass media art of the ’80s and ’90s, which, according to Casey Reas was one of the pre-conditions for NFTs.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Neo-Dada." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 29, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: The Origins of Computer Art

This series of experimental artworks by Ben Laposky was generated on analogue equipment by photographing oscilloscope patterns created by electronic circuits. He called these resulting images “Oscillons.” These works are among the earliest examples of electronically generated images. In 1953, Laposky exhibited fifty Oscillons as photographs, kinetic oscilloscope displays, light boxes and movies at the Sanford Museum in Cherokee, Iowa.

cite.label: Popper, Frank. Art of the Electronic Age, 78. New York: Thames and Hudson, 1997.

body: Grace Hopper is one of the most important pioneers in the development of computer programming. Hopper pioneered the concept of automatic programming and in 1952 she developed the first compiler (A-0). Most critically, Hopper was the first to write programs in words rather than symbols. By 1957 she had completed FLOW-MATIC (B-0), the first English-language business data processing compiler. FLOW-MATIC became the main model for COBOL, specified in 1959 by a committee drawn from computer manufacturers and the Pentagon on which Hopper served as technical adviser, as a language capable of operating on different types of computers. Hopper thus enabled general computer languages, which would profoundly and irrevocably impact computer technology in the long-term. In the short-term, it also helped to significantly expand the number of people who could interact with computers.

cite.label: Sammet, Jean E. "The Real Creators of Cobol." IEEE Software 17, no. 2 (2000): 30-32. https://doi.org/10.1109/52.841602

body: This important example of kinetic sculpture, dated c.1953 by Tate, was created using a set of rules (i.e. “the smallest black elements should hang as far from the largest black elements as possible, not directly beneath them”) to create random motion. Kinetic sculpture was a critical predecessor to the digital motion of electronic (generative) art.

cite.label: Popper, Frank. Art of the Electronic Age, 12. New York: Thames and Hudson, 1997.

body: Plans mobiles (Mobile Planes), made from 1953 to 1955, perfectly illustrates a “new energy from the possibility of movement” in art. These reliefs of flat metal and painted wood mounted on pivots, turned by hand, serve as an important step in the development of interactive art.

img.credit: Tania Sheko. “Pol Bury, Plans mobiles, 1953-55.” Flickr. flickr.com

body: As proto-video art, this exhibition was an important precursor to electronic art. It combined experimentally composed music with surrealistic visuals. As told by Jikken Kōbō co-founder, Yamaguchi Katsuhiro: “Asahigraph editor Izawa Tadasu introduced Kōbō to the Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation (later SONY), which had developed an “autoslide projector,” a slide projector with synchronized sound. The group established a relationship with the company, and the Kōbō members worked together to create an audiovisual piece for this device.”

img.cap: Jikken Kōbō members Hiroyoshi Suzuki and Katsuhiro Yamaguchi photographed in 1953, the year the group made its four synchronised-sound Autoslide pieces with the Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation (later Sony).
img.credit: Hiroyoshi Suzuki and Katsuhiro Yamaguchi, 1953. Via Monoskop.

body: Exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity, this ahead of its time cybernetic sculpture anticipated interactivity in electronic art. An interactive installation that translated musical input into visual displays of colored lights, Musicolour utilized sensors to detect the pitch, rhythm, and dynamics of the music, generating a real-time visual representation of the audio. Musicolour blurred distinctions between music and visual art, pioneering the concept of synesthesia and the integration of different sensory modalities in artistic experiences. This groundbreaking work inspired subsequent generations of artists and researchers to explore the intersection of sound and visuals, leading to the development of generative art practices that create dynamic and interactive audio-visual compositions. Musicolour’s influence can be seen in the use of real-time data and the integration of multiple sensory inputs in contemporary digital generative art.

cite.label: Haque, Usman. "The Architectural Relevance of Gordon Pask." Architectural Design 77, no. 4 (2007): 54-61. https://doi.org/10.1002/ad.487

img.cap: Gordon Pask, Musicolour, 1953–57. Archival photograph of the sound-responsive machine.
img.credit: Gordon Pask. Archival image reproduced in dOCUMENTA (13), Musicolour research entry by Wayne Clements. Photographer not identified. Image source.
img.alt: Black-and-white archival photograph of the Musicolour apparatus, showing rows of dials, electrical components and large circular mechanisms in an open cabinet.
creator: Gordon Pask

body: Founded by Jiro Yoshihara, Gutai was a radically experimental movement even by today’s standards. Its experimental approach to art-making combined with its interest in technology, participation and conceptual art paved the way for later artists in Japan to explore generative processes and techniques.

img.cap: The cover of the 1959 Gutai issue of the Turin journal Notizie: Arti Figurative, showing Saburō Murakami bursting through stretched paper screens — the earliest European publication devoted to Yoshihara's group.
img.credit: Cover of Notizie: Arti Figurative, Gutai issue, Galleria Notizie (Luciano Pistoi), Turin, 1959. Photograph by Potassio23, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

body: Bense’s Aesthetica, foundational to computer art history, established the theoretical foundation of computer art. Bense proposed a systematic approach to analyzing the form and structure of art, emphasizing the importance of mathematical and logical principles. Bense’s ideas would later greatly influence his students, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake, as well as the direction of the computer art pioneers’ work.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Max Bense." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 18, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: The Brazilian movement rejected strict adherence to the orthodoxy of purity, science, and math. Grupo Frente was interested in representing organic, nonfigurative forms. They promoted increased creative intuition in geometric abstraction. The movement was instrumental in the development of Concrete Art and geometric abstraction, particularly in Latin America.

With both young artists desperate to leave Belleville, they got creative. “This can’t go on; we can’t live there any more; it’s filthy; we’ll find a studio,” Vera remembers François remarking at the time. Leveraging the area’s bad reputation, they orchestrated a flat swap with “drunks” eager for proximity to bars. The move landed them in a seventh-floor Rue de Gergovie apartment with a studio and panoramic Paris views. Together, Vera and François, dubbed a “two-headed painter,” collaborated until 1960, when François shifted to a research career. In the late '50s and early '60s, Vera explored solo creativity, first investigating the machine imaginaire.

cite.label: Peter Bauman, “Molnár’s Paris,” Le Random, 26 February 2024, section 4. Rue de Gergovie Apartment and Studio. Includes Vera Molnár’s recollections from Interview with Vincent Baby (Manuella éditions, 2022), p. 37, quoted in the article.

img.credit: Photograph: François Molnár. Vera Molnár archives; courtesy of the artist, as credited in Peter Bauman, “Molnár’s Paris,” Le Random, 2024. Image source.
img.alt: Vera Molnár seated by a tall studio window in 1954, with geometric artworks on the wall behind her.

body: In 1954, Douglas Ross created the “Scope Input Program.” This program made for Whirlwind computers was the first example of hand-drawing with a computer. In 1951, the Whirlwind began operating at MIT as part of the first demonstration of a graphics display on a vectorscope screen. It was thus the first computer that operated in real time. SAGE operators selected targets with a light gun, a pointing device carried over from Whirlwind. This enabled a form of rudimentary hand drawing on a computer. IBM built a duplexed AN/FSQ-7 computer, descended from MIT’s experimental Whirlwind, for each SAGE direction centre. These two projects were significant to the development of computing and digital generative art as they demonstrated the viability of cathode-ray tube displays.

cite.label: Ross, Douglas T. "A Personal View of the Personal Work Station: Some Firsts in the Fifties." In A History of Personal Workstations, edited by Adele Goldberg, 68. New York: ACM Press, 1988.

img.cap: The circular cathode-ray-tube monitor used with MIT's Whirlwind, the display on which the first real-time computer graphics — and, with the light gun and Douglas Ross's Scope Input Program, the first hand-drawing on a computer — were made.
img.credit: Circular monitor display for the Whirlwind computer. Collection of the Computer History Museum, Mountain View.

body: John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky, along with Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, organized the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence. This seminal event marked the birth of AI as a field of study. The conference itself did actually take place in 1956, as proposed. The now legendary proposal and subsequent conference by the titans of the field asserted that machines could simulate every aspect of learning and intelligence, laying the foundation for decades of AI research—and winters. The term “artificial intelligence” was coined with this document and the project brought together leading minds to explore machine learning, neural networks, and more, setting the stage for the scientific and artistic explorations of a field at its birth.

cite.label: McCarthy, John, Marvin L. Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude E. Shannon. "A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, August 31, 1955." AI Magazine 27, no. 4 (2006): 12. https://doi.org/10.1609/aimag.v27i4.1904

img.cap: John McCarthy's typescript “An approach to the artificial intelligence problem,” signed in his own hand, from the papers Ray Solomonoff kept at the Dartmouth summer project.
img.credit: John McCarthy, “An approach to the artificial intelligence problem,” Dartmouth Summer Research Project, 1956. Ray Solomonoff Dartmouth papers, raysolomonoff.com.

body: Victor Vasarely’s seminal Yellow Manifesto envisioned a synthesis between art and technology to enhance art’s accessibility through mass production. His manifesto links the Constructivist research of the Bauhaus to Op Art, Kinetic Art, New Tendencies and contemporary generative art. Vasarely believed that technology could spearhead the accessibility of art by rejecting the concept of a single work. Instead, Vasarely proposed making art more reproducible. This move played an important role in the gradual dematerialization of art, a critical step in the development of electronic, performance and conceptual art. The concept of mass produced art would also greatly influence Pop Art and remains central to the broadening collector base that generative art today enjoys. Vasarely also questioned the “lone genius” artist which would inspire the New Tendencies groups of the ’60s, especially Group de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV). GRAV was significantly influenced by Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto and included two of generative art’s most timeless icons: Vera Molnár and François Morellet. Other members included Yvaral Vasarely (Victor’s son) and Julio Le Parc.

img.credit: Victor Vasarely / Galerie Denise René, 1955. Image: Michèle Vasarely Foundation; reproduction photographer not identified. Image source.
img.alt: Yellow printed sheet with Vasarely’s manifesto on the left and the Le Mouvement exhibition cover on the right.
creator: Victor Vasarely

body: John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence” in a proposal for a Dartmouth College study written with Marvin Minsky (Harvard University), Nathaniel Rochester (IBM) and Claude Shannon (Bell Telephone Laboratories). According to the proposal, “the study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” The proposal also included an early hypothesis on the connection between randomness, intuition and creativity: “A fairly attractive and yet clearly incomplete conjecture is that the difference between creative thinking and unimaginative competent thinking lies in the injection of some randomness. The randomness must be guided by intuition to be efficient. In other words, the educated guess or the hunch include controlled randomness in otherwise orderly thinking.” The workshop took place the following year and is considered the official beginning of the field.

img.cap: Ray Solomonoff's own fanned copies of the Dartmouth documents, with the title page of “A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence” — the August 1955 typescript that coined the term — visible beneath Shannon's proposal and above Newell and Simon's plans.
img.credit: Ray Solomonoff's copies of the Dartmouth proposals, 1955–56. Ray Solomonoff Dartmouth papers, raysolomonoff.com.

body: The April 1955 exhibition at the Galerie Denise René, in which Vasarely was central, launched both Op and Kinetic Art, while inspiring the New Tendencies group GRAV. It’s thus a pivotal moment in the history of generative art. Le Mouvement included Yaacov Agam, Pol Bury, Alexander Calder, Marcel Duchamp, Robert Jacobsen, Jesús Rafael Soto, Jean Tinguely and Victor Vasarely. The exhibition corresponded to the principles laid out in his “Yellow Manifesto.” An intense period of experimentation in media and production choices followed the exhibition. The manifesto and this exhibition helped lay the groundwork for both electronic art and the digitization of generative art.

img.cap: Le Mouvement / The Movement / Paris 1955, the catalogue published for Galerie Denise René’s New York exhibition in 1975, revisiting the 1955 Paris exhibition.
img.credit: Roger Bordier; Éditions Denise René. © Roger Bordier. Photograph © ZKM | Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe, photo: Franz J. Wamhof. Image source.

body: This legendary outdoor exhibition featured radical concepts that were a decade ahead of their time. The central innovative concept that concerns generative art’s development was the direct encouragement of audience participation and interactivity. GRAV would not bring this concept to European audiences until the mid ’60s.

body: This mobile kinetic sculpture is considered the first cybernetic sculpture. CYSP is short for “CYbernetic SPatiodynamic.” The piece, whose electronic brain was built by engineers at Philips, used microphones, wheels, motors and cells that responded to their environment. The structure could, for instance, navigate between obstacles. Schöffer’s work sought to merge the theories of cybernetics with artistic creation. His Lumino-Kinetic sculptures used light, movement and sound to demonstrate kinetic principles.

body: A precursor to C. P. Snow’s “two cultures” thesis of 1959, The New Landscape in Art and Science was a book that attempted to combat the growing pessimism in the art world towards the mixing of art and science. Kepes, the prominent figure in the development of computer and digital art, explored the intersections between art, science and technology. He sought to focus on where science and art intersected, laying out ideas about visual perception, patterns and the relationship between art and nature. The publication was poorly received by his contemporaries yet, critically, it illustrated the growing rift between science and art.

cite.label: Kepes, Gyorgy. The New Landscape in Art and Science. Chicago: Paul Theobald, 1956.

img.credit: György Kepes. The New Landscape in Art and Science. 1956.

body: Following the first exhibition, the group continued to enhance audience participation. It even anticipated the communal drawing practices of the net art community. It was an additional important contribution by Gutai to the development of interactive art as well.

body: The Gutai member’s best known work was constructed by fashioning vividly painted light bulbs into a dress. The piece consists of only light bulbs and their cords. A re-imagination of the traditional kimono, Electric Dress represented modern Japan’s embrace of the new in society as well as art. This aligned perfectly with the aims of the Gutai group, seeking a radical departure from the past, which had been largely marked by turmoil and war for decades. The group also sought to blur the lines between everyday life and art, another way Tanaka’s Electric Dress exemplifies the movement. It would not be for several more years before European groups like New Tendencies began making such calls. An important predecessor to electronic art, the dress embraced elements central Tanaka’s career and Gutai: change, movement and interactivity. It was also an important step in the development of electronic art as an interactive Light sculpture.

img.credit: "flickr.com by flickr.com is licensed under creativecommons.org.

body: A hugely important moment in Chance Dance and with a score by John Cage, Suite for Five is a Neo-Dada classic. According to the Art Story:

“Cunningham and Cage relied heavily upon chance in the creation of this work, citing that both the score and the choreography were determined by random operations like counting the imperfections in a piece of paper.”

body: Conceived in 1954, the programming language of early computer art, Fortran (FORMula TRANslator) is one of the oldest high-level programming languages. It made code more comprehensible to scientists, mathematicians and, of course, artists.
Originally developed by IBM, it became the first computer language standard and is one of the most influential software products in history. It is still in use today.
Fortran was also essential to the early development of computer art. Early pioneers like Vera Molnár, Manfred Mohr and many others used the language to create algorithmic art in the 1960s and 1970s.
The Victoria and Albert Museum on Fortran:

“Fortran is used in works including Dominic Boreham’s IM21 (B5) P0.5 3.X.79. Early computer programmes were stored on punched cards, including Manfred Mohr’s P032 (Matrix Elements). Written by the artist in Fortran, this programme instructed a plotter device to produce the drawing P-32 (Matrix Elements).”

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Fortran." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified April 4, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: This consequential paper by Brooks, Hopkins, Neumann and Wright outlines how a computer can be used as a system to create art.

cite.label: Brooks, F. P., Jr., A. L. Hopkins, Jr., P. G. Neumann, and W. V. Wright. "An Experiment in Musical Composition." IRE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-6, no. 3 (September 1957): 175-182.

body: Chomsky’s epochal book influenced both mid-century computational theory and artificial intelligence by introducing the concept of Transformational-Generative Grammar, “the most significant development in linguistic theory and research in the 20th century.” Generative Grammar seeks to explain how humans are able to produce and understand an infinite number of grammatically correct sentences. The theory proposes that language is innately hardwired into the human brain and that there are underlying rules or structures that govern the way in which sentences are formed. It has had a significant impact on computational theory. The theory has inspired the development of algorithms and computational models that attempt to simulate the way in which humans generate and understand language.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Syntactic Structures." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 27, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Founded by Otto Piene and Heinz Mack in Düsseldorf, four years before New Tendencies, Zero was inspired by the notion of starting over (hence the name). The group grew throughout the ’50s and early ’60s into an international movement of artists and architects who sought to create a new form of art that was both rational and objective, focusing on a work’s materials. Also associated with the Gutai movement in Japan, Zero rejected traditional art forms and embraced new technologies, focusing on geometric abstraction and kinetic art. As Margit Rosen would write on the connection between New Tendencies and computer art: “New Tendencies’ idea of art as research, the endeavor to enforce a constructive, rational, demystified art and to overcome the gap between current art practices and processes in science and technology, as well as the wish to stop the art market from defining artistic aims and methods, made it possible to open this art movement to the world of computing technology and its own band of practitioners.”

img.cap: The fourth Evening Exhibition in the atelier at Gladbacher Strasse 69, Düsseldorf, September 26, 1957.
img.credit: Photograph: Hans Salentin. Archive of the ZERO foundation, via ZERO ABC. Image source.
img.alt: Black-and-white view of paintings hanging on the walls of a brick studio, with a cloth-covered piano in the foreground.
creator: Hans Salentin

body: The spiritual successor to the Bauhau closed after 24 years primarily due to financial difficulties. It had been opened in 1933 by John A. Rice, who hired the Bauhaus’s Josef Albers. The college’s faculty and staff over the years included some of the most impactful artists of the twentieth-century such as Anni and Josef Albers, Walter Gropius, Merce Cunningham, John Cage, Robert Motherwell, Dorothea Rockburne, Cy Twombly, Robert Rauschenberg, Susan Weil, Franz Kline, Aaron Siskind, Willem and Elaine de Kooning and Mary Caroline Richards.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Black Mountain College." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified March 24, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: According to Hamilton, an early progenitor of Pop Art: “Pop Art is: Popular (designed for a mass audience), Transient (short-term solution), Expendable (easily forgotten), Low cost, Mass produced, Young (aimed at youth), Witty, Sexy, Gimmicky, Glamorous, Big business” Similar words have been used to derisively describe the on-chain art of today.

creator: Richard Hamilton

body: Environments, precursors to “happenings” as well as the Performance and Installation Art of the ’60s-’70s, were large-scale, immersive installations intended to engage all of the senses of the viewer. Kaprow believed that art should be experienced rather than observed, and his Environments were designed to create an interactive and participatory experience for the viewer.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Allan Kaprow." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 25, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: In this talk, Duchamp explained the importance of chance in the creative act. He deemed that both the artist and the participant partook in chance creation, anticipating the work of Eco several years later “The Open Work” by Umberto Eco.

“All in all, the creative act is not performed by the artist alone; the spectator brings the work in contact with the external world by deciphering and interpreting its inner qualifications and thus adds his contributions to the creative act.”

img.cap: Marcel Duchamp, “The Creative Act,” ARTnews 56, no. 4, June–July–August 1957, page 28.

body: Mathews, computer music pioneer, developed the computer music composition language on an IBM 704 while at Bell Labs. MUSIC I was the first demonstration of computer synthesized music. Mathews himself described the development: “Computer performance of music was born in 1957 when an IBM 704 in NYC played a 17 second composition on the Music I program which I wrote. The timbres and notes were not inspiring, but the technical breakthrough is still reverberating.”

cite.label: Max Mathews, Horizons in Computer Music, 1997, Indiana University.

body: This piece by Malina, pioneer of Lumino-Kinetic art, demonstrates the development of the Lumino-Kinetic movement towards electronic art.

body: Rich, of the Applied Physics Laboratory, Johns Hopkins University, wrote one of the earliest examples of using a computer program for graphic design, according to Herbert W. Franke. This was of wave patterns for textiles.

body: Information Theory and Esthetic Perception by Abraham A. Moles, later professor at Strasbourg University, was an early, important work on information aesthetics. Moles combined Shannon’s information theory with aesthetics. While Bense’s generative aesthetics focused on an artwork’s aesthetic value, Moles was interested in models of perception and semiotics or symbolic communication. This book posits that pleasure, beauty, and artistic response are the result of informational processes, which can be mathematically analyzed and understood. According to Margit Rosen, “it inspired the development of strategies to develop procedures of programming as a precondition for the production of art.”

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Abraham Moles." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 23, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: After Hitchcock hired John Whitney to create the opening animation for his film, Vertigo, Whitney used a WWII-era “M5 gun director” targeting computer that required five people to operate. This device was used because it could rotate endlessly and was thus able to move in relation to a pendulum that was generating the spiral compositions. Saul Bass collaborated with Whitney to design the analog-computed animated sequence.

cite.label: Ozturk, Selen. "Vicious Circle: John Whitney and the Military Origins of Early CGI." Bright Lights Film Journal, March 15, 2023.

body: Foreshadowing the plotter, the Swiss kinetic sculptor’s key piece in the history of chance in art, Méta-matic No. 8, was an animated sculpture made from found material. The piece was exhibited at the legendary The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age. link This piece itself was actually a drawing machine, constantly producing an abstract drawing on its own. Tinguely said: “The machine is above all an instrument which permits me to be poetic. If you respect the machine, if you enter into a game with the machine, then perhaps you can make a truly joyous machine; by joyous I mean free.” The piece, like much of Tinguely’s work, also questioned the role of the artist’s hand in an artwork’s production and the art object itself. This work also further demonstrates the role of Kinetic Art in the development of computer art as well as an example of proto-digital generative art.

cite.label: Hultén, K. G. Pontus. The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age, 166. New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1968.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Jean Tinguely." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified January 8, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Kilby demonstrated his device in 1958, Noyce’s design following in 1959. The integrated circuit was a breakthrough in electronics that sparked the miniaturization of the industry. The large size of previous circuit iterations, such as tubes and transistors, caused frequent faulty connections and failures. The entire circuit of a computer (transistors, capacitors, resistors, wires, …) could now be made with silicon and could fit on a single board.

img.cap: A museum replica of the first integrated circuit, the germanium chip Jack Kilby demonstrated at Texas Instruments in September 1958, photographed at the Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum.
img.credit: Replica of Jack Kilby's first integrated circuit, Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum. Photograph by Florian Schäffer, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

body: A rebuke of gestural art and extension of modern art’s abstraction, Minimalism emerged in the late ’50s with exhibitions such as Frank Stella’s Black Paintings at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. But Dorothy Miller’s 16 Americans, also at MoMA, established the importance of the young movement.

Julesz’s “Two Image Random Dot Stereograms” were 2 side-by-side randomly generated dot images. When viewed through a stereoscope they created the sensation of depth. Julesz displayed these patterns on a screen and developed the procedure at Bell Labs.

cite.label: Julesz, Bela. "Binocular Depth Perception of Computer-Generated Patterns." Bell System Technical Journal 39, no. 5 (1960): 1125-1162.

body: The exhibition was held at the Museum of Applied Arts in Vienna, presenting the experimental images of the then physicist-artist, Herbert W. Franke. Franke experimented with a variety of machines and technical methods including, analog computers, oscillograms and X-ray machines.

body: One of the earliest computer graphics output devices sold and the first drum plotter printer, the CalComp 565 could produce large-scale drawings with precise lines, becoming a popular tool for computer artists. CalComp would come to dominate the plotter market by the end of the next decade, proving to be indispensable to the development of computer art.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2022. "Calcomp plotter." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 25, 2022. en.wikipedia.org.

body: To protest nuclear war and showcase his values of spontaneity and randomness, Metzger creates his first acid paintings. This form of material generative art is created by spraying acid onto sheets of nylon. This produces rapidly changing shapes as the nylon dissolves. The work is thus auto-creative as well as auto-destructive. Metzger along with Max Bense was instrumental in the development of generative art. He and Bense “envisioned art as a laboratory for imagining how computers could defy their militaristic origins and be structured according to alternative logics—the eruptive spontaneity of the creative act, for example, or the mutually beneficial, horizontal processes of communication and collaborative action.”

img.cap: Gustav Metzger, Manifesto of Self-Destructive Art, 1959. Manuscript.
img.credit: Gustav Metzger. The Gustav Metzger Foundation Collection, Tate Archive, London. Image source: Gustav Metzger Foundation. Image source.
img.alt: Creased manuscript sheet headed Manifesto, SDA, Self Destructive Art, with handwritten statements and the date 1959.
creator: Gustav Metzger

body: C.P. Snow’s “Two Cultures” lecture was a call to bridge the divide between the sciences and the humanities, embodied by the multi-disciplinary computer art. Snow argued that this gap, and the lack of understanding between the two groups, was detrimental to society’s progress. In the 1960s and 1970s, “The Two Cultures debate framed much of the early criticism and reception of computer art.” Early computer artists were primarily from a scientific background and viewed art from a technical perspective, leading to their work being dismissed by traditional artists and critics.

cite.label: Taylor, Grant D. When the Machine Made Art: The Troubled History of Computer Art, 16. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2014.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "C. P. Snow." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified July 1, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Kaprow’s seminal exhibition was the first Happenings and coined the term as art form. Happenings were avant-garde, interactive art events that paved the way for Performance Art and Fluxus. The exhibit itself consisted of a sequence of 18 loosely scripted events or “happenings” that took place in six different areas of the Reuben Gallery in New York. The happenings, designed to be experienced by a small audience, also encouraged audience interaction in the work. In one section of the exhibit, actors walked around the space holding umbrellas and chanting a series of words and phrases. In another section, performers created a large wall made of newspapers, which the audience was invited to tear down. Along with Gutai in Japan and GRAV in Paris, happenings anticipated many concepts of the contemporary digital generative art space: the work was designed to challenge traditional notions of art and spectatorship, breaking down barriers between art and everyday life. It was also a participatory and immersive experience with audience members becoming active collaborators in the creation of the art.

img.cap: Allan Kaprow with the “Sandwich Man” during 18 Happenings in 6 Parts at the Reuben Gallery, New York, photographed by Fred W. McDarrah on 2 October 1959.
img.credit: Fred W. McDarrah, Allan Kaprow with “Sandwich Man,” in 18 Happenings in 6 parts, Reuben Gallery, 2 October 1959. The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles.

body: Gullar’s manifesto advocated for a new kind of art that rejected the formalism of traditional concrete art and embraced a more humanistic, participatory approach. It called for a more organic, intuitive, and emotional art that engaged the senses and emotions of the viewer, serving as an important development in the histroy of South American geometric abstraction.

cite.label: Mol, Elias Perigolo. “Experiência Neoconcreta: O Suplemento Dominical e o Manifesto Neoconcreto.” MODOS: Revista de História da Arte 7, no. 1 (2023): 105. https://doi.org/10.20396/modos.v7i1.8671412

Jornal do Brasil

body: This key development in the pre-history of computer-generated literature was an early use of a computer to generate text. Lutz’s “stochastic texts” were produced at Stuttgart when Max Bense was there developing Aesthetica. The texts were determined by a syntactical scheme, random generator and frequency criteria on a Z22. Lutz’s usage of stored words provided Bense with ideas for Aesthetica.

cite.label: Thomas Dreher, History of Computer Art. p. 49

body: This important example in the history of chance in art consists of simply a found piece of driftwood that happened to look like something else. Dubuffet noticed the piece after thinking the natural shape resembled a head and the barnacles resembled hair. He burned a few additional holes and placed the work on a pedestal. Dubuffet believed that natural forms, simplicity and rawness endowed his work with greater authenticity.

img.cap: Jean Dubuffet, Tête barbue (Bearded Head), 1959. Driftwood with barnacles.
img.credit: Jean Dubuffet. Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, Washington University in St. Louis. Gift of Florence S. Weil, 1982 (WU1982.16.2). Image: Kemper Art Museum. Image source.
img.alt: A barnacle-covered piece of driftwood with two dark eye-like hollows and a long tapering beard, mounted on a black base.

body: Meaning the “imaginary computer,” Molnár’s “machine imaginaire” is the now famous concept that she developed to imagine a computer to expand her creative process. The hypothetical machine allowed her to systematically create works that included all the possible combinations of forms she wished. Now based in Paris, It would take nearly another decade, 1968, before Molnár would gain access to an actual computer.

img.cap: Vera Molnár, Quatre éléments distribués au hasard, 1959. Graphite and adhesive plastic film on cardboard.
img.credit: © Adagp, Paris. Centre Pompidou, MNAM-CCI, AM 2008-189. Photograph: Georges Meguerditchian / Dist. GrandPalaisRmn. Image source.
img.alt: Square composition of black vertical, horizontal, and diagonal line segments distributed across a pale field.
creator: Vera Molnár
Georges Meguerditchian

body: Popularized in today's imagination by DeepMind's AlphaGo, machine intelligence and games has a long history. In fact, in the early 1950s, very early computers around the world started playing basic games, like tic-tac-toe with real people.

First was the 1950 Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, where Josef Kates’s Bertie the Brain played tic-tac-toe against visitors. Then in 1951, Ferranti’s Nimrod played nim at the Festival of Britain’s Science Exhibition in London. Both machines were built for that one specific game only, though.

In contrast, Dietrich Prinz used the general-purpose Ferranti Mark I at the University of Manchester to solve simple mate-in-two chess problems in November 1951. Finally, between 1951 and 1952 Christopher Strachey (of love-letter fame) wrote a draughts program that looked a few moves ahead and valued positions by the pieces left on the board. Given wrong input, it printed “I REFUSE TO WASTE ANY MORE TIME. GO AND PLAY WITH A HUMAN BEING.”

We have always welcomed the challenge from machines, particularly as they wobbled clumsily in their early days. Now, in the second quarter of the twenty-first century, artificial intelligence can beat humans at essentially any digital task or game. The test has turned to robotics as the next human vs machine game frontier.

img.cap: A replica of Nimrod, the machine that played nim at the 1951 Festival of Britain, at the Computerspielemuseum in Berlin.
img.credit: Replica of Ferranti’s Nimrod (1951) at the Computerspielemuseum, Berlin. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: As described by Jasia Reichardt herself at Le Random (“The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room”), on January 14, 1958, the mathematician I. J. Good, a one-time colleague of Alan Turing, spoke at the Gaberbocchus Common Room in London.

Franciszka and Stefan Themerson had opened the club in 1957 in the Maida Vale basement of their Gaberbocchus Press so that artists and scientists could meet. Good asked whether a machine could make probability judgments. He imagined one built from partly random networks of model neurons, rewarded for a correct judgment with a chemical that lowered the thresholds of the neurons it had just used. Computers and Automation printed the talk in 1959. In a 1965 paper Good called such a machine "ultraintelligent." He wasn't far it seems.

img.cap: Franciszka and Stefan Themerson, who ran the Gaberbocchus Common Room where Good spoke.
img.credit: Franciszka and Stefan Themerson. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: The quest for machines that did more than just blindly follow instructions in binary determinacy, for machines that actually think, is a long one, covered many times on this Timeline (Lady Lovelace’s Objection, the Turing Test, the Homeostat).

For instance, in January 1956 Herbert A. Simon told his class, "Over Christmas Allen Newell and I invented a thinking machine." With Cliff Shaw at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, they had built the Logic Theorist, a program that searched for proofs in symbolic logic using heuristics modeled on human problem solving.

At the now legendary Dartmouth workshop that summer, where the term "artificial intelligence" was coined, the three described IPL, the list-processing language in which they wrote it. By 1957, running on RAND's JOHNNIAC computer, the Logic Theorist had proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in chapter 2 of Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell's Principia Mathematica.
Logic with learning would prove a valuable combination in the decades ahead.

img.cap: JOHNNIAC, the RAND computer on which the Logic Theorist ran, now at the Computer History Museum.
img.credit: RAND’s JOHNNIAC computer at the Computer History Museum, Mountain View. CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Computerized text and language games have gone hand in hand with the systems and generative art for centuries.

But a big step took place in 1954 when philosopher Margaret Masterman founded the Cambridge Language Research Group to study machine translation, then outside the curriculum of every English university. The informal circle became the Cambridge Language Research Unit (CLRU) in 1956. Early members included the plant scientist Richard H. Richens, the mathematician Lady Hoskyns and the linguist M. A. K. Halliday.
In 1968 Cybernetic Serendipity showed Masterman's Computerized Japanese Haiku, made with Robin McKinnon Wood at the CLRU: a poem frame whose slots an operator filled, sometimes from the thesaurus.

body: The heart of AI has been tugged by academia, industry and most worryingly the military for the entirety of its existence. Here we see that pattern play out in action as McCarthy and Minsky's legendary AI research lab had roots in academia before jettisoning to DARPA and the military industrial complex.

In 1959 John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky founded the Artificial Intelligence Project at MIT, the institute's first coordinated AI research, within the Research Laboratory of Electronics and the Computation Center.

AI was vague from the start, as no written proposal was ever made. When the laboratory's director, Jerome Wiesner, asked what they needed, McCarthy recalled, "we asked for a room, two programmers, a secretary and a keypunch." Wiesner also had them supervise some of six mathematics graduate students. But this was a huge development as McCarthy's LISP was implemented there.
Later, in 1963, the lab joined the DARPA-funded Project MAC. The MIT AI Lab later split off from Project MAC and in 2003 merged with the Laboratory for Computer Science to form CSAIL.

img.cap: John McCarthy in 2006, nearly fifty years after he and Marvin Minsky founded the MIT project.
img.credit: John McCarthy at Stanford, 2006. CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Back at MIT, Oliver Selfridge of its Lincoln Laboratory, presented "Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning" at the Symposium on the Mechanisation of Thought Processes at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, England, in November 1958; the proceedings appeared in 1959. It was an exciting time for computing, before it had really been pigeonholed into less experimental roles from the late '60s onwards (until maybe around 2010 with the advent of deep learning proper).

Selfridge's model for learning to recognize patterns had four levels of "demons." Data demons stored the image and computational demons computed features from it. Cognitive demons weighed that evidence and shouted; a decision demon picked the loudest. It learned by adjusting the weight given to each feature and by culling and breeding its feature demons through a kind of natural selection.
Not neural networks but "demons," one can still see how prevalent statistical weights are in machine learning.

img.cap: A redrawn diagram of Selfridge’s four levels of demons: data, computational, cognitive and decision.
img.credit: Diagram of Oliver Selfridge’s Pandemonium model, after his 1959 paper. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Depending on how it goes with AI, the perceptron could end up being one of history's most important concepts, well, ever basically.

Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron is essentially the first neural network and a monumental step in the story of deep learning AI art. The perceptron is also a bit of a tragic tale. A decade later, deep learning AI's anti-hero Marvin Minsky published Perceptrons, a book that critics of neural networks would point to in order to discredit the field or deny funding. It was thought of as proof that those pesky neural networks just didn't work. Machines couldn't learn (at least not that way). So the perceptron itself marks the beginning of neural networks and also partly explains why if this idea came out in 1958, it only really exploded around 2010. There are many reasons why like data and compute needing to catch up with theory. But that theory barely even existed, largely because of Minsky and his dividing of the AI field from about 1969 to 2010.

Rosenblatt himself though was a research psychologist at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York. He described the perceptron in a 1957 report and in Psychological Review in 1958. It modeled the brain as sensory, association and response units that learn to sort shapes into classes. In July 1958 the U.S. Office of Naval Research (And, yes, you knew the military industrial complex was going to be involved, didn't you?) demonstrated it on an IBM 704: after 50 trials, the computer taught itself to tell cards marked on the left from those marked on the right. In other words, it was already demonstrating some very early effectiveness.
Rosenblatt called it "the first machine which is capable of having an original idea." The human idea itself was certainly original.

img.cap: A U.S. Navy photograph of the Mark I Perceptron, the machine built to run Rosenblatt’s design, with an operator at its image sensor.
img.credit: The Mark I Perceptron, about 1960. U.S. Navy photograph (USN 710739), National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: It's not hard to understand why DeepMind's first thought with AI was games. As several (El Ajedrecista) other (the chess-playing Turk) moments (the first game programs) have mentioned, games and machine learning have a long history. But in the early '50s it's remarkable these machines could even approach playing a game like checkers, several decades before Deep Blue started beating chess world champions.

Legendary ML computer scientist Arthur Samuel, who IBM credits with coining the term machine learning, wrote his first checkers program for the IBM 701 in 1952. His paper “Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers,” in the July 1959 IBM Journal of Research and Development, described two methods: saving positions the program had scored and adjusting its scoring formula’s weights. Those weights changed as one copy, Alpha, played another, Beta. A computer, Samuel wrote, “can be programmed so that it will learn to play a better game of checkers than can be played by the person who wrote the program.”

img.cap: The console of an IBM 701, the machine for which Samuel wrote his first checkers program in 1952.
img.credit: Operator’s console of the IBM 701. CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: That language is mathematical and conceivably can be automated like a calculator is no new thought as many pre-Modern language "versifiers" and other tools have taught us. But still something is particularly prescient about this Roald Dahl mid-century description of something approaching an LLM.

Dahl's collection of short stories Someone Like You, published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1953, includes ours of interest: “The Great Automatic Grammatizator.” Its hero, Adolph Knipe, an engineer who has helped build a giant computing machine, decides that English grammar follows rules almost as strict as mathematics and builds a machine that writes stories and novels to order. He and his employer, Mr. Bohlen, flood the market, then pay real authors to put their names to machine-written books and stop writing. In a tragic twist, the narrator, a writer, is one of the few who refuses, and his children go hungry.
It's a bleak tale of an author's insecure anxieties decades too soon. But it seems to be coming truer by the day in the 2020s.

body: It's almost comforting that over seventy years ago, we were similarly tantalized by the seductive power of machinic intelligence. As soon as it became clear that machines were excellent at following instructions, we seemed to expect them to also be able to think, on their own. We can see this impulse from a book in France that helped bring the ideas of cybernetics to the continent and, globally, popularize the idea that machines were somehow capable of thinking.

The French science journalist Pierre de Latil published La Pensée artificielle with Gallimard in 1953; it appeared in English in 1956 as Thinking by Machine: A Study of Cybernetics. Writing for general readers, de Latil explained the new science of feedback and control through the machines of its founders, among them W. Ross Ashby's homeostat and W. Grey Walter's electronic tortoises, and asked whether such devices could be said to think. The American edition even carried a foreword by Isaac Asimov.
Are machines really intelligent, really thinking or just fooling us into believing they are? These are persistent questions stretching back decades. Are we closer to an answer today?

cite.label: Pierre de Latil. La Pensée artificielle. Paris: Gallimard, 1953. English edition: Thinking by Machine: A Study of Cybernetics. Translated by Y. M. Golla. London: Sidgwick and Jackson, 1956.

body: The UK's answer to the 1956 Dartmouth AI conference, this symposium continued the budding field's momentum and mostly open-minded spirit,  as one of the first international meetings on artificial intelligence after Dartmouth.

As for the event itself, it took place in November 1958 at Britain's National Physical Laboratory in Teddington. The conference took place over four days and its theme was the Mechanisation of Thought Processes. Her Majesty's Stationery Office would go on to publish its proceedings in two 1959 volumes.

John McCarthy presented “Programs with Common Sense,” proposing a program that would reason from stated facts, and Oliver Selfridge presented Pandemonium, a model of pattern recognition by competing units, mentioned previously on this timeline. It was a veritable all-star lineup with Marvin Minsky, Grace Hopper, Donald MacKay and Albert Uttley all speaking.

The late-50s weren't entirely free as it was still a bit political who even got invited to these conferences with certain regrettable omissions, chiefly Rosenblatt. However, these were still mostly drama-free days in AI research. But drama would plague the field in ten years' time with Minsky's Perceptrons book all but splitting the field ideologically into connectionist and symbolic camps.
